lesson.title: Bonds Are a Bank Account, Not a Light Switch
lesson.summary: Forming a chemical bond always releases energy while breaking one always requires energy, and the net energy change of a reaction is simply the balance between the bonds broken in the reactants and the bonds formed in the products.
lesson.body:
Every chemical bond represents a drop in potential energy compared to the separated atoms, which means the act of forming a bond always releases energy into the surroundings, usually as heat, making bond formation an exothermic process. The reverse process, breaking a bond, requires exactly that same amount of energy to be put back in, making bond breaking an endothermic process. This is really just the energy concept applied specifically to chemical bonds: since a bond exists in the first place because it lowered the system's energy, undoing that bond has to raise the energy back up by the same amount, and forming it again releases that same amount back out.

The amount of energy involved in forming or breaking a particular bond is called its bond energy, sometimes called bond dissociation energy, and it is defined as the energy required to break one mole of that specific bond in the gas phase. A hydrogen to hydrogen single bond has a bond energy of 436 kilojoules per mole, meaning it takes 436 kilojoules to break apart one mole of H2 molecules into individual hydrogen atoms, and forming H2 from separate hydrogen atoms releases that same 436 kilojoules per mole back out. Stronger bonds have larger bond energies and release more energy when they form, a chlorine to chlorine single bond, by comparison, has a bond energy of only about 242 kilojoules per mole, reflecting a weaker bond that releases less energy on formation and requires less energy to break.

This bookkeeping becomes genuinely useful when applied to entire chemical reactions rather than single bonds. Every reaction can be thought of in two stages: first, breaking all the bonds in the reactants, which costs energy, and second, forming all the bonds in the products, which releases energy. The overall energy change of the reaction is simply the difference between those two totals: energy of bonds broken minus energy of bonds formed. If more energy is released forming the new bonds than was spent breaking the old ones, the reaction is exothermic overall and releases net energy, usually as heat. If breaking the old bonds costs more than forming the new ones gives back, the reaction is endothermic overall and absorbs net energy from the surroundings.

This framework is exactly what explains why ionic compounds form even when the initial electron transfer step is unfavorable, a case covered when discussing ionic bonds directly. Turning gaseous sodium and chlorine atoms into Na+ and Cl- ions costs a net 147 kilojoules per mole, since sodium's ionization energy, 496 kilojoules per mole, is not fully offset by chlorine's electron affinity of negative 349 kilojoules per mole. That step alone would make sodium chloride formation look unfavorable, but it is only one part of the full energy accounting, the much larger release of energy that happens as the ions come together and form new ionic bonds throughout a solid crystal lattice more than makes up the difference, giving an overall favorable, exothermic process for the reaction as a whole. Bond formation energy, applied consistently across every bond broken and formed in a process, is what ultimately determines whether a chemical change releases energy to its surroundings or demands energy from them.
